title: Phase-transition-driven ferroic response in 2D CuMnP_2Se_6 under ultra-low electric fields

paper_content.abstract: Low-field electric control of magnetic phase transitions is critical for the development of energy-efficient spintronic and non-volatile memory technologies. Yet, the weak magnetoelectric coupling in most known two-dimensional multiferroics hinders their practical implementation. Here, using crystal structure prediction and high-throughput first-principles calculations, we identify four previously unexplored bimetallic thio(seleno) phosphate multiferroics, XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X=Cu, Au), all exhibiting robust in-plane spontaneous polarization—contrasting with the predominantly out-of-plane behavior in this material family—which effectively mitigates depolarization effects. In particular, CuMnP2Se6 hosts two stable C2-symmetric ferroelectric phases with opposite in-plane polarizations and distinct magnetic orders. Remarkably, an electric field as small as ~0.001 V/Å can simultaneously reverse the polarization and induce an antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition. The associated barrier is exceptionally low (~49 meV/f.u.), yielding a sizable magnetoelectric coefficient of ~0.04 G⋅cm/V. These results highlight a viable strategy for realizing electric-field-driven magnetism in intrinsic two-dimensional multiferroics under experimentally feasible conditions.
paper_content.introduction:
Electric-field control of magnetism offers a promising route to reduce energy consumption in spintronic and memory devices, paving the way for low-power, non-volatile information technologies that could transform future computing paradigms1–3. To date, two primary mechanisms have been extensively investigated: (i) electric-field-induced magnetization switching4–6, and (ii) electric-field-driven magnetic phase transitions7–10. The former enables binary logic operations through spin-orbit torque-driven reversal of magnetization, whereas the latter involves switching between distinct magnetic phases—such as ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM)—offering dynamic tunability between writable and interference-robust memory states. Realizing such functionality requires material systems where electric polarization and magnetic order are strongly coupled and reversibly tunable under experimentally accessible conditions.

Multiferroics, which simultaneously host two or more ferroic orders—such as magnetism, ferroelectricity, or ferroelasticity—within a single phase11, offer a natural platform for realizing intrinsic magnetoelectric (ME) coupling. However, electric-field-induced magnetic phase transitions in existing multiferroics remain rare, primarily due to the generally weak coupling between electric and magnetic order parameters. As a result, polarization reversal alone is often insufficient to drive a magnetic transition12–22. An alternative strategy leverages van der Waals heterostructures composed of 2D magnets and ferroelectrics, where electric control of magnetism arises from interfacial ME effects6,23–27. However, such heterostructures often suffer from weak interfacial coupling and require precise lattice matching and stacking control, posing significant challenges for scalable fabrication and long-term device stability28. Thus, identifying single-phase 2D multiferroics with strong intrinsic ME coupling has become a central pursuit in the field29–31. Despite increasing interest, such materials remain scarce. Moreover, the substantial switching barriers (>several hundred meV/f.u.) observed in most reported materials demand high electric fields (>0.1 V/Å), creating a major bottleneck for their application in energy-efficient electronics.

In this study, we report four stable 2D bimetallic thio(seleno) phosphate (BMTP) multiferroics, XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au), each exhibiting two inequivalent C2-symmetric phases with opposite in-plane spontaneous polarizations, which helps mitigate depolarization fields. Notably, CuMnP2Se6 features two such C2 phases with distinct magnetic ground states—FM and AFM. An ultralow electric field of ~0.001 V/Å can drive a structural transition between these phases, thereby reversing the polarization and switching the magnetic order simultaneously. The transition is characterized by a remarkably low switching barrier (~49 meV/f.u.) and a sizable ME coupling coefficient (~0.04 G⋅cm/V). These findings demonstrate strong ME coupling and ultralow switching barriers in 2D BMTPs, highlighting their potential as a promising platform for electric-field control of magnetic phase transitions under experimentally accessible conditions.
paper_content.results:
In-plane polarization in CuMnP2Se6
The BMTPs with the general formula XYP2(S/Se)6 (X, Y = transition metals), crystallize in van der Waals layered structures and represent a versatile family of emerging piezoelectric, ferroelectric, and multiferroic materials32–35. Their compositional flexibility—achieved by varying X and Y elements such as Cu, Ag, In, Cr, and V—enables systematic tuning of electronic, ferroelectric, and magnetic properties36–39. Dimensional reduction to monolayers via mechanical exfoliation offers an effective pathway to tailor ferroic behaviors40–43, with improved control over polarization and magnetic states.

A prototypical 2D BMTP structure, exemplified by CuCrP2S6, consists of metal cations intercalated within a hexagonal framework composed of ethane-like [P2S6]4− units with C3 symmetry. The Cu1+ and Cr3+ cations alternately occupy interstitial sites, forming a secondary honeycomb sublattice. Each Cr3+ ion is centered within an octahedron of six S2− ligands, accounting for the magnetic behavior, while the out-of-plane displacement of Cu1+ ion gives rise to spontaneous polarization44. The out-of-plane (OOP) polarization switching proceeds through a nonpolar (NP) intermediate phase which possesses D3 symmetry. Notably, a broad range of 2D BMTPs can be derived by substituting different transition-metal species into this structural motif36–39,45.

To further explore the structural landscape of 2D BMTP family, we performed ab initio structure searches for CuMnP2Se6 using the CALYPSO method46–51. We selected Mn as the Y-site transition metal because Mn3+ possesses a high-spin d4 electron configuration. In an MnSe6 octahedral environment, the Mn3+ ion adopts a t2g3 eg1 configuration, which is well known to produce a strong Jahn-Teller instability (Supplementary Fig. 1). The singly occupied eg orbital (dz2 or dx2−y2) directly overlaps with the ligand p orbitals, leading to pronounced structural distortion of MnSe6 octahedra, involving tetragonal compression or tetragonal elongation (Supplementary Table 1). This situation stands in sharp contrast to other 2D BMTPs such as CuCrP2Se6 (Cr3+, t2g3), CuVP2Se6 (V3+, t2g2) and CuFeP2Se6 (Fe3+, t2g3 eg2), where the transition-metal ions are Jahn-Teller inactive. Consequently, the strong Jahn-Teller activity of Mn3+ may facilitate the emergence of new structural prototypes that are inaccessible to other transition metals.

As expected, two low-energy polar prototypes with C2 symmetry were identified, referred to as the D-type and C-type phases, characterized by the formation of Cu-Mn dimer-like units and -Cu-Mn-Cu-Mn-chain-like configurations, respectively. In contrast to conventional BMTP structures, where the X cation typically displaces vertically from the center of its octahedron, the X ion in both newly identified phases remains centered, accompanied by slight in-plane displacements. These displacements give rise to spontaneous in-plane polarization. Specifically, the D-type and C-type structures exhibit opposite in-plane polarization directions along [110] and [110], respectively. This behavior stands in sharp contrast to most previously reported 2D BMTP multiferroics, which typically display OOP polarization36,44.

The distinct polarization behavior in these systems arises from two key factors: Jahn-Teller activity and symmetry-forbidden s-d coupling44. The Jahn-Teller active Mn3+ ion (t2g3 eg1) lifts the eg orbital degeneracy, leading to tetragonal compression in the D-type phase and tetragonal elongation in the C-type phase (Supplementary Table 1). These distortions generate an in-plane anisotropic local potential, which drives lateral Cu displacement. In contrast, in BMTP compounds such as CuCrP2S6, where the Jahn-Teller effect is weak, the nearly symmetric crystal field fails to create such a gradient potential, thereby suppressing in-plane polarization.

Meanwhile, the local approximate Oh symmetry around the Cu+ ion in CuMnP2Se6 forbids s-d coupling because the s and d orbitals belong to different irreducible representations (Supplementary Table 2). This symmetry-forbidden s-d hybridization contrasts with the symmetry-allowed s-d coupling in CuInP2S6, which drives the OOP polarization44. This forbidden s-d coupling in CuMnP2Se6 is further supported by the projected density of states (PDOS) and band-decomposed charge density (Supplementary Fig. 2). Therefore, the combination of strong Jahn-Teller distortion and symmetry-forbidden s-d coupling collectively determines the emergence and stabilization of in-plane polarization in CuMnP2Se6. A more detailed discussion is provided in the Supplementary Information.

High-throughput screening and identification of in-plane ferroelectric phases and magnetic ground states
Having identified four structural prototypes, we employed high-throughput first-principles calculations to systematically investigate the possibility of D-type and C-type structures within this material family. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, we considered compounds with the formula XYP2(S/Se)6 (X=Cu, Ag, Au; Y=Mn, Tc), generated via targeted elemental substitution. The X-site elements (Cu, Ag, Au) were chosen as monovalent cation owing to their good displacive nature and can easily displace from the octahedral center, thus generating ferroelectric polarization. The Y-site transition metals were selected to ensure a high-spin t2g3 eg1 configuration (e.g., Mn3+ and Tc3+), which naturally leads to Jahn-Teller activity and strong coupling among orbital, lattice, and spin degrees of freedom.

A total of 48 candidate structures were initially generated based on the four structural prototypes. After full structural relaxation, 5 OOP-polarized phases were found to be unstable and spontaneously transformed into NP phases. The potential energy profile of Cu-ion displacement further confirms the energetic preference for the NP phase (Supplementary Fig. 3). Consequently, the final dataset comprises 43 stable configurations: 7 OOP, 12 NP, 12 D-type, and 12 C-type phases (Fig. 2a). Among these, all XYP2(S/Se)6 compounds in the D-type and C-type phases, except AgMnP2Se6, possess lower energies than their NP and OOP counterparts (Supplementary Table 3). Because the total energies of AgMnP2Se6 in different prototypes are nearly degenerate, indicating a structurally marginal system, it was excluded from subsequent phonon calculations.

Phonon spectrum calculations reveal that CuMnP2(S/Se)6 and AuMnP2(S/Se)6 are dynamically stable in both D-type and C-type configurations, whereas AgMnP2S6 is stable only in the C-type configuration (Supplementary Figs. 4, 5). We then determined the magnetic ground states of the dynamically stable compounds, excluding AgMnP2S6 since only its C-type phase is stable and no meaningful comparison between two polar phases can be made. For the remaining systems, we considered one FM and two possible AFM configurations (Supplementary Fig. 6). Interestingly, unlike other compounds where both polar phases prefer AFM ordering, CuMnP2Se6 displays two polar phases with different magnetic ground states—one FM and one AFM (Fig. 2b). This unique behavior allows an electric-field-induced polarization reversal to simultaneously trigger a magnetic phase transition between FM and AFM states. Consequently, we focus our subsequent discussion on CuMnP2Se6.

Distinct structural motifs, electronic properties and magnetic ground states in D-type and C-type CuMnP2Se6
Figure 3a and b show schematic structural diagrams of the D-type and C-type phases of CuMnP2Se6 in a 2×2×1 supercell, with the P and Se atoms omitted for clarity. In the D-type phase, Cu and Mn atoms form dimer-like units with a nearest-neighbor distance of 3.43 Å, and the distance between neighboring dimers is 3.82 Å. In the C-type phase, Cu and Mn atoms form chain-like units with a nearest-neighbor distance of 3.64 Å along the chain, and the distance between neighboring chains is 3.75 Å. The C-type phase is slightly lower in energy than the D-type phase by ~4 meV/f.u.

The cohesive energy of CuMnP2Se6 is calculated using the equation Ecoh = (Etot − ECu − EMn − 2EP − 6ESe)/10, where Etot is the total energy of 2D CuMnP2Se6, and ECu, EMn, EP, and ESe are the total energies of isolated Cu, Mn, P, and Se atoms, respectively. The cohesive energies for both D-type and C-type phases are similar, ~ -3.92 eV/atom, suggesting that both structures are thermodynamically stable and potentially synthesizable. Furthermore, Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations at 100 K confirm the thermal stability and in-plane long-range polarized order of CuMnP2Se6 (Supplementary Fig. 7).

The spin-polarized band structures show that both the D-type and C-type phases are semiconductors with indirect band gaps of 0.18 eV and 0.16 eV, respectively (Fig. 3c, d). Spin-orbit coupling has a negligible effect on the electronic structure and is therefore excluded from subsequent calculations (Supplementary Fig. 8). Spin density calculations show that the spin moments are mainly localized on Mn ions (Supplementary Fig. 9). The PDOS confirms that the spin polarization near the Fermi level mainly comes from Mn 3d orbitals. The formal spin moments for Mn and Cu are 4 μB and 0 μB, respectively, consistent with their expected valence states of Mn3+ and Cu1+. The overlap between the Mn 3d and Cu 3d orbitals is observed below the Fermi level in PDOS (Supplementary Fig. 10). In fact, the overlap originates from the strong hybridization of Mn 3d-Se 4p and Cu 3d-Se 4p states, making the Cu and Mn d states appear to overlap.

In the D-type phase, the valence band maximum is primarily derived from Mn dx2−y2 orbitals, while the conduction band minimum mainly originates from Mn dz2 orbitals (Fig. 3e). In contrast, the C-type phase shows the opposite orbital contributions to the valence and conduction bands (Fig. 3f). The calculated onsite energies of Mn d orbitals (Supplementary Table 4) confirm that the dx2−y2 orbital lies lower in energy than the dz2 orbital in the D-type phase, whereas the reverse holds for the C-type phase. This distinct orbital ordering enhances Mn dx2−y2 -Se pxy hybridization in the D-type phase and Mn dz2 -Se pz hybridization in the C-type phase (Fig. 3g, h; Supplementary Fig. 11). Structurally, the D-type phase exhibits tetragonal compression, which energetically favors the formation of Mn-Cu dimer-like units, whereas the C-type phase shows tetragonal elongation, stabilizing a chain-like -Mn-Cu-Mn-Cu- arrangement (Supplementary Table 1; Fig. 3a, b). This structural response reflects the system’s tendency to minimize total energy under different orbital hybridization conditions. In turn, these distinct structural configurations tend to modulate the Mn-Mn exchange pathways, which may lead to different magnetic ground states in the two phases.

The spin Hamiltonian is defined as H = − ∑i,j J1 Si Sj − ∑i,k J2 Si Sk, where J1 and J2 are the nearest-neighbor and next-nearest neighbor magnetic exchange parameters between Mn ions, respectively22,52–54. The summation i, j, and k run over all the Mn sites. S is the formal magnetic moment of Mn ion. The positive and negative J values represent the FM and AFM coupling, respectively. By energy mapping analysis on the considered magnetic configurations (Supplementary Fig. 6), the calculated J1 and J2 for the D-type are 4.70 meV and 1.30 meV, respectively, indicating the FM ground state. In contrast, the calculated J1 and J2 for the C-type are 4.67 meV and -4.72 meV, respectively, indicating the AFM ground state. Monte Carlo simulations show that the magnetic critical temperature for FM D-type and AFM C-type phases are ~31 K and ~18 K, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 12).

We further investigated the impact of the Hubbard U parameter on magnetic ordering and orbital-level splitting for both D-type and C-type phases, finding that the overall qualitative trends and key conclusions are robust over a broad range of U values (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6).

Electric-field-induced magnetic switching in CuMnP2Se6
Berry phase calculations yield an in-plane polarization of 0.9 × 10−10 C/m along the [110] direction for the D-type phase and 0.7 × 10−10 C/m along the [110] direction for the C-type phase (Supplementary Figs. 13, 14). Born effective charge analysis55,56 gives corresponding values of 0.4 × 10−10 C/m for the D-type phase and 0.2 × 10−10 C/m for the C-type phase, in good agreement with those obtained from the Berry-phase method. These values are larger than those reported for other DTMPs12,36,57,58, such as AgBiP2Se6 (1.2 × 10−12 C/m), CuCrP2S6 (0.79 × 10−12 C/m), AuZrP2S6 (9.74 × 10−12 C/m), and comparable to other 2D multiferroics13,16,59–61, such as (CrBr3)Li (0.92 × 10−10 C/m), and γ-AlOOH (0.85 × 10−10 C/m).

The polarization in both the D-type and C-type phases can only be switched by 120° through an in-plane rotation of 120° or 240° (Fig. 4a, b; Supplementary Fig. 15a, b). This process can also be understood as a lateral displacement of Cu ions. The corresponding energy barriers for ferroelectric switching are ~36 meV/f.u. for the D-type phase and ~32 meV/f.u. for the C-type phase. In contrast, a 180° polarization reversal within the same phase (either D-type or C-type) is prohibited, as the positions of Cu and Mn ions cannot be interchanged directly.

However, 180° polarization reversal remains feasible through an electric-field-induced phase transition between the D-type and C-type structures, accompanied by the migration or removal of Cu atoms (Fig. 4c; Supplementary Fig. 15c). Specifically, reversing the applied electric field—e.g., from [110] to [110]—can trigger a transition between the two phases, owing to their opposite polarization orientations. This electric-field-driven structural transformation simultaneously induces a magnetic phase transition, owing to the distinct magnetic ground states of the D-type and C-type structures. Figure 4c illustrates the energy barrier associated with this phase transition, which proceeds via an intermediate structure that closely resembles the D configuration and can be regarded as the NP phase (Supplementary Fig. 16). The calculated barriers for both D-to-C and C-to-D transitions are nearly identical, ~49 meV/f.u. This value is nearly an order of magnitude lower than those reported for other 2D multiferroics exhibiting electric-field-induced magnetic transitions29–31. Notably, the D-to-C transition can also be triggered by applying tensile strain (Supplementary Fig. 17).

The ME coupling coefficient can be estimated as α ≈ μ0 |ΔM|/Ec, where μ0 is the vacuum permeability, ΔM is the magnetization change per unit cell associated with polarization switching, and Ec is the coercive electric field62. As is well known, a direct evaluation of Ec from first-principles is very challenging, since in real ferroelectric materials, polarization reversal is typically dominated by domain-wall motion and defect-mediated processes rather than homogeneous switching, and Ec is also strongly temperature dependent63. Therefore, we adopted a more reasonable reference value based on experimentally accessible ferroelectric systems to estimate Ec. The values of energy barrier (4.9 meV/atom) and polarization (13 μC/cm2 for the D-type phase and 9 μC/cm2 for the C-type phase, assuming an effective thickness of 7 Å) in CuMnP2Se6 are comparable to those reported for ferroelectric Hf(Zr)1+xO2 thin films (7.3 meV/atom; 22.5 μC/cm2)64. Thus, we adopt the experimentally reported coercive field of Hf(Zr)1+xO2, 65 kV/cm, to estimate the ME coupling coefficient of CuMnP2Se6. This yields α ≈ 0.04 G⋅cm/V, which exceeds those of bulk multiferroic Fe/BaTiO3 (~0.01 G⋅cm/V)62, and 2D WReCl36 (~0.02 G⋅cm/V)29, indicating the strong ME coupling.

To evaluate the feasibility of in-plane electric-field-driven structural transitions between the D-type and C-type phases, we investigate the field-dependent total energies of both configurations (Fig. 4d). The two phases exhibit opposite responses: an electric field along the [110] direction stabilizes the C-type phase, while a field along [110] favors the D-type phase. Strikingly, an ultralow field of ~0.001 V/Å along [110] is sufficient to render the D-type phase more stable than its C-type counterpart, enabling an electric-field-induced C-to-D transition. The critical field lies well within experimentally accessible limits8,65, highlighting the potential of CuMnP2Se6 for practical multifunctional device applications.

In summary, we identify four stable 2D multiferroics of the form XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au), each exhibiting two inequivalent C2-symmetric polar phases with opposite in-plane polarization directions, based on crystal structure prediction and high-throughput first-principles calculations. Jahn-Teller activity and symmetry-forbidden s-d coupling are identified as the two primary driving forces for the emergence of in-plane polarization in these systems. Notably, in CuMnP2Se6, the two polar phases differ not only in their polarization orientation but also in their magnetic ground states (FM and AFM), enabling electric-field-driven switching of both ferroic orders. The ultralow energy barrier (~49 meV/f.u.) and critical switching field (~0.001 V Å−1) render these coupled transitions experimentally accessible. These findings demonstrate a viable route for electric control of magnetism in single-phase 2D multiferroics and provide new insights into ferroic coupling in the BMTP family, with promising implications for low-power, non-volatile device applications. This work also opens a promising avenue for exploring ultralow-field electric control of magnetism enabled by Jahn-Teller-assisted phase-transition mechanisms.
paper_content.methods:
First-principles calculations were performed based on density functional theory66 via the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)67,68 using the generalized gradient approximation with the projected augmented wave method69 with a 450 eV plane-wave energy cutoff. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof function was adopted for the exchange-correlation functional70. A Γ-centered k-point grid of 11 × 11 × 1 was applied for sampling the Brillouin zone. The energy and force threshold for structural optimization are 10−7 eV and 0.001 eV/Å, respectively. An effective Hubbard U of 4 eV for Mn 3d, Cu 3d and Tc 4d orbitals71,72 was applied following the Dudarev formulation73. Phonon spectra were calculated using the finite displacement method implemented in the PHONOPY code74. The temperature-dependent effective potential method was used to determine the influence of thermal effects on phonon spectra75. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations were performed utilizing the Nosé-Hoover chain thermostat for 5 ps with a time step of 1 fs with 3 × 3 × 1 supercell. Climbing image nudged elastic band calculations76 were performed to determine the energy barriers for ferroelectric switching. The polarization was estimated using the Berry phase approach77. An in-plane electric field was applied by imposing a finite homogeneous field using the perturbation expression after discretization approach78,79. The maximally localized Wannier functions are constructed by using the WANNIER90 code80.

The particle-swarm optimization method within the evolutionary algorithm, as implemented in the CALYPSO code46–51, was employed to search for the lowest-energy structures of the CuMnP2Se6 monolayer. Unit cells containing one and two formula units were considered. In the initial generation, random structures with specific symmetries were constructed by generating atomic coordinates through crystallographic symmetry operations. Local optimizations were carried out using the VASP code67,68 with the conjugate-gradient method and terminated when the Gibbs free-energy change was smaller than 1 × 10−4 eV per cell. After each generation, 40% of the low-energy structures were selected to construct the next generation through particle swarm optimization, while the remaining 60% were randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique based on the bond-characterization matrix was employed to avoid duplication and enhance population diversity, which is crucial for efficient global searching. In total, the search typically sampled 1200 structures (40 generations × 30 structures).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors J. Chen et al., in their manuscript “ Phase-Transition-Induced Ferroelectric and Magnetic Switching in Two-Dimensional CuMnP2Se6 under Ultra-Low Electric Fields”, have investigated four compounds XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au) belonging to the family of bimetallic thio(seleno)phosphates using density functional theory based calculations. Their main observations are the presence of in-plane electric polarization in these four compounds as opposed to the out-of-plane polarization reported earlier for other members of the family. The authors also report that a tiny electric field can be used to switch the polarization direction in CuMnP2Se6 along with the magnetic order.
I observe some serious issues with the conclusions drawn here by the authors which I outline below.
1. The non-polar intermediate state D3, between the D-type and C-type phases, is metallic (see Fig. S11). Therefore, an electric field cannot be used to switch the direction of polarization. Another related question is when the non-polar D3 phase is metallic, how was the polarization quantum calculated? It is not possible to calculate it by following the standard procedure.
2. The AIMD snapshots at 300K after 10 ps for both D and C-type (Fig. S4) show a significant change in the bond lengths which is the primary requirement for the structure to be called D-type or C-type (Fig. 3 (a) & (b)). Thus, at 300K, D and C-type phases of the structure don’t survive and there should be no net in-plane polarization given the loss of order in the bond lengths of the structures.
3. Why a weak Jahn-Teller effect will give rise to out-of-plane polarization whereas a strong Jahn-Teller effect will give rise to in-plane polarization is not clear at all. The orbital resolved DOS presented in Fig. S7 shows Mn dz2 and dx2-y2 orbitals both present below the Fermi level. A strong Jahn-Teller effect would have split these two orbitals widely.
4. How does distinct orbital ordering in C and D-type phases lead to the respective structural distortions? How do they give rise to different magnetic ground states for C and D-type phases? No explanation is provided. Moreover, the DOS in Fig. 3 (e) shows substantial contribution of both dz2 and dx2-y2 orbitals in the valence band whereas the band character plot shows dominant dx2-y2 contribution.
5. The claim that there is no bonding like interaction between Cu and Mn is not very convincing. There seems to be a very strong overlap between Cu and Mn d states in the valence band (as seen in PDOS of Fig. 3(c), 3(d) and S7) which directly indicates a strong hybridization between Cu and Mn. The ELF plot also shows some bonding like behaviour particularly in the C-type structure. Also, the crystal field around Cu changes in a similar manner as that around Mn typical for a Cu-Mn bonding interaction (see Fig. 1(c), 1(d)). The non-polar phase PDOS (Fig. S11(b)) also shows a very strong Cu-Mn hybridization.
6. If Cu-d orbitals do not hybridize with Mn-d orbitals as claimed, why doesn’t it exhibit s-d interaction and hence, an out-of-plane displacement as is the case with the materials without an eg electron (e.g., CuCrP2S6).
7. How are the temperatures for phonon calculations in Fig. S2 decided? What about the dynamic stability at higher temperatures? The last phonon spectrum for AuMnP2S6 seems to have imaginary frequencies.
8. There are a couple of typos. ( ‘insensitive’ instead of ‘sensitive’ and ‘eg’ instead of ‘t2g’ in the Supplementary mat.).
Finally, I would like to mention that no new concept has been presented in this manuscript. The concept as well as the analysis is exactly similar to the work by Meiling Xu et al. , Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 067602 (2020) (ref. [29] of the manuscript). Only the compound studied is different.
In view of the above serious issues, I can not recommend the manuscript for publication in the highly reputed journal Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The work of Chen et al. uses a combination of first principles methods to identify a particular ferroelectric system, CuMnP2Se6, with two opposite polarizations, but with different magnetic ground states. Notably, a small electric field reverses the polarization and induces an AFM to FM transition. I find the work very interesting, clear, well-written, and of potential technological importance.
There are some small weaknesses that can be improved.
1. Fig. 1, please add colored spheres in the figure to clarify the atoms types.
2. Page 2, paragraph 5. Please justify the selection of X= Cu, Ag, Au, Y = Mn, Tc for the targeted elemental substitution. Why not consider other transition metals? What values of U were used for Mn and Tc?
3. Page 2, paragraph 5. How was "the number of candidate structures 48" found? Using 3 for X, 2 for Y, 2 for S, Se, and 2 for C, D type I find 24.
4. Page 2, paragraph 6. When computing the FM and AFM ground states. Did the author consider large supercells for AFM configurations? If so, how large? How was the supercell size cut-off chosen? Is there any experimental evidence to support any of these magnetic ground states in this or other BMTP systems?
5. Page 2, paragraph 7. The sentence "In the D-type phase... Cu-Mn dimer with a bong length ... shorter than the alternating Cu-Mn bond.." was difficult to understand. What is the alternating bond? Please identify the alternating bond in Fig. 3.
6. In Page 3, paragraph 3, the position of different Mn d orbital characters are discussed and shown in Fig. 3. What is the axis of quantization used to project the orbitals? Along the global z axis or along one of the octahedral axis? In the latter case, specify which one. Figs. 3g and 3h are not clear, are these in 2D or 3D? Are d_xy, d_yz, d_xz degenerate?
7. Page 3, paragraph 5. How does the polarization computed for CuMnP2Se6 compare to the value computed for CuInP2S6 in this work?https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.108.L180101Please specify the polarization is in-plane.
8. Page 4, paragraph 4. Since the values of U and P for CuMnP2Se6 are comparable to those of Hf(Zr)1+xO2, the authors adopt a coercive field of 65 kV/cm. However, how does this compare with a coercive field estimated as E_c ~ dE / (PV), where dE, P, V are the energy difference between nonpolar and polar structures, and P, V are the polarization and volume of the polar structure?
9. In Page 5, paragraph 1. The two C2-symmetric opposite polarizations have different values, correct? If so, please report both values.
I recommend acceptance after minor revisions.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I don't find the work suitable for publication in Nature Communications. This work contains only the theoretical results, and it lacks the experimental evidence of the proposed structures. I still have some comments that may be helpful to improve the quality of the manuscript.
In Figure 1, it's difficult to differentiate the crystal structures (eg, top views in a and b, both views in c and d). I suggest highlighting the main difference among the structures in Figure 1 and explaining it clearly in the caption/main text.
The authors say, 'out-of-plane displacement of Cu1+ gives rise to spontaneous polarization.' Are they referring to the atom shown in yellow in Figure 1 (a)?
Justify the sentence 'In an MnS(Se)6 octahedral environment, this t32ge1g configuration causes strong Jahn–Teller distortions, facilitating the emergence of new structural prototypes not accessible with other transition metals.' Why can't this happen for other TMs?
The authors mentioned D-type and C-type phases in the manuscript. The author should provide some context and relevant sources of other phases as well (such as A-type, B-type phases, if they exist), instead of directly using C or D-type phases. This will help the readability of the paper.
What are the other unstable structures? Do they comprise Tc? Can you comment on why Tc - radioactive element - was considered in the calculations?In Figure 2(a), do they mean XYP2(S/Se)6 instead of XYP2S(Se)6?
USPEX has also been very popular in predicting novel crystal structures. The author should comment on their choice of CALYPSO over USPEX.
Figure S1 (a, b) in Supporting Information: What are the displacement values? Do x-axes represent the number of images created?
In Figure S2 in Supporting Information, what do (2) and (4) represent? Also, are they simulated at different temperatures?
There is no consistency in atomic colors in the crystal structures throughout the manuscript, which should be fixed.
The authors should provide references for every equation/formula they have used in the manuscript. For example, the spin Hamiltonian on page 3, the ME coupling coefficient on page 4. reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The research focus on the electric field control of magnetic phase transitions, specially in cases where the necessary electric fields are small for practical reasons. The manuscript is very well written and all results look correct. The research lacks experimental results and focus only on first principle calculations and modeling with a spin Hamiltonian. However, the authors did a phonon analysis (with and without thermal effects), together with molecular dynamics to confirm thermal stability. Those are already the methods necessary within first principles to access the viability of the materials experimentally. Additionally, the authors used several methods to access the properties of the materials, such as: Berry phase method to calculate the in-plane polarizations; Wannier analysis for the orbital ordering; and NEB calculations to investigate different phase transitions. I conclude then that the manuscript is suitable for publication at Nature Materials after reviews:
1 - In Figure 1, it is very difficult to understand the structural differences between the NP, C and D types (OOP is more obvious). The authors could improve the understanding by explicitly indicating which of the metal atoms are displaced to create the in-plane polarization. Also using different colors for top and bottom S/Se atoms can help.
2 - The authors used DFT+U and tested some values of U, but they used a rather modest value of U throughout the manuscript and SI. Also they only compared the energy ordering for a small range of U (either 3 or 4eV).
a) What is the effect of energy ordering for U < 3eV? What happens for much larger values of U (perhaps up to 8 eV)? Specially Mn can be quite tricky to deal with.
b) Is the orbital ordering also affected by the U values? I believe that higher values will increase the separation of the orbitals, but there is also a possibility of changing the ordering in case the occupation pattern shifts. What happens for U = 0 eV? Is it still S = 2 or does it go to S = 1?
3 - By changing the U to lower values the authors could also investigate better the interactions between the Cu and Mn ions. It is reasonable to consider less strong localized orbitals, leading to more hybridization between Cu and Mn ions.
4 - Can the authors comment further on the structures that present negative frequencies in the phonon spectra? What are the modes associated to them?

mechanism of electric-field control of magnetic phase transitions in type-I multiferroics,
and to provide a candidate material capable of realizing this mechanism. To advance
the potential applications of electric-field control of magnetism, however, it remains
essential to reduce the required external electric field. The present study is exactly
centered on this issue and, at the same time, reveals new underlying physics.
(i) We show that an electric field as small as 0.001 V Å−1 can induce the FM–AFM
phase transition in CuMnP Se , which is nearly two orders of magnitude lower than the
2 6
∼
critical field reported in the PRL work. This extremely low threshold makes the

polarization in members of the BMTP family, in clear contrast to the predominantly
out-of-plane polarization commonly observed in this material family. This in-plane
configuration is particularly advantageous because it mitigates depolarization effects,
enhances ferroelectric retention, and facilitates integration into planar device
architectures.

fundamental microscopic factors governing the polarization direction and
magnetoelectric coupling in this system. This provides a clear and generalizable
physical picture and may guide the search for other low-field multiferroics with coupled
ferroic orders.
Taken together, these advances represent a substantial conceptual and physical
extension of the previous PRL work, moving toward experimentally realizable low-
field electric control of magnetism in 2D multiferroics. We believe these findings
constitute a genuine advance that aligns well with the scope and standards of Nature
Communications.

Authors’ Reply: Thanks for the question. To determine the magnetic ground states, we
constructed 2 × 2 × 1 supercells for all antiferromagnetic (AFM) configurations, which
allowed us to capture both nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor exchange
interactions within the layer. To verify convergence with respect to supercell size, we

magnetic ordering in this system.

on bimetallic thio(seleno)phosphates (BMTP) [Sci. Bull. 66, 233 (2021), J. Phys.:
Condens. Matter 35, 395501 (2023)], where similar exchange pathways govern the
magnetic behavior. Experimental studies on related monometallic
thio(seleno)phosphates (e.g., MnPSe [Phys. Rev. B 103, 024414 (2021), Nat.
2 6

range magnetic order, lending further confidence to the theoretical framework
employed in this study.

COMMENT:
I don't find the work suitable for publication in Nature Communications. This work
contains only the theoretical results, and it lacks the experimental evidence of the
proposed structures. I still have some comments that may be helpful to improve the
quality of the manuscript.
Authors’ Reply: We fully agree that the combination of theory and experiment
provides the most powerful route for advancing materials discovery. Indeed, if our
predicted material could be experimentally synthesized and its ferroelectric and FM–
AFM switching under ultralow electric fields verified, it would represent a significant
step forward toward next-generation information storage and spintronic devices.
However, performing such synthesis and characterization is currently beyond the
experimental capabilities of our group, as all co-authors focus on the development of
computational methods and theoretical modeling of materials.
Nevertheless, we are confident that the predicted phase can be experimentally realized,
since many materials predicted using our self-developed CALYPSO code, such as H O-
3 3
Lett. 128, 106001 (2022)], LaH [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 027001 (2019)], and CaH
10 6
[Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 167001 (2022)], have already been successfully synthesized,
several of which were originally proposed by the authors of this work.
Furthermore, our current work offers several key findings beyond the specific material
prediction:
(i) First identification of in-plane ferroelectricity in the BMTP family: Previous
experimental works on bimetal thio(seleno)phosphate BMTP compounds, such as
CuInP S [Nat. Commun. 7, 12357 (2016)] and CuCrP S [Nat. Commun. 14, 7304
2 6 2 6
(2023)], have revealed out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization. To the best of our
knowledge, our work is the first to predict robust in-plane ferroelectric polarization in
this family, which effectively mitigates the depolarization fields that often suppress out-
of-plane ferroelectricity in ultrathin layers. Moreover, in-plane ferroelectricity is
particularly attractive for nonvolatile memory and low-power electronic switches, as it
enables device geometries that are compact, scalable, and nondestructive in operation,
as recently demonstrated in in-plane ferroelectric systems such as SnTe and In Se
2 3
[Science 353, 274-278 (2016); Sci. Adv. 4, eaar7720 (2018)]. These features make the
proposed structure a realistic and experimentally meaningful target for synthesis and
device applications.
(ii) Proposal of the microscopic mechanism of in-plane ferroelectricity: We uncover
Jahn-Teller activity and symmetry-controlled s-d coupling as the fundamental
microscopic factors governing the polarization direction and magnetoelectric coupling
in this system. This provides a clear and generalizable physical picture that goes beyond
the material-specific case and may guide the search for other low-field multiferroics
with coupled ferroic orders.
(iii) Experimental accessibility of the predicted electric-field-driven magnetic
switching: Ultralow-field control of magnetism through an electric-field-driven phase
transition makes the system highly appealing for experiments, as the required switching
field (~0.001 V/Å) can be easily achieved under typical laboratory conditions. For
instance, electric fields up to ~0.1 V/Å have already been achieved experimentally in
systems such as CrI [Nat. Mater., 17, 406-410 (2018)] and WTe -based ferroelectric
3 2
heterostructures [Nat. Nanotech. 18, 861-866 (2023)].
These findings establish a comprehensive and predictive theoretical framework that we
believe fully justifies publication of our work in Nature Communications.

switching pathways by 120° and 180°.
The 120° switching process can be realized through an in-plane rotation of 120°

switching can still be achieved through an electric-field-induced phase transition
between the D-type and C-type structures, accompanied by the migration or removal of
Cu atoms.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Low-field electric control of magnetic phase transitions is critical for the development of energy-efficient spintronic and non-volatile memory technologies. Yet, the weak magnetoelectric coupling in most known two-dimensional multiferroics hinders their practical implementation. Here, using crystal structure prediction and high-throughput first-principles calculations, we identify four previously unexplored bimetallic thio(seleno) phosphate multiferroics, XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X=Cu, Au), all exhibiting robust in-plane spontaneous polarization—contrasting with the predominantly out-of-plane behavior in this material family—which effectively mitigates depolarization effects. In particular, CuMnP2Se6 hosts two stable C2-symmetric ferroelectric phases with opposite in-plane polarizations and distinct magnetic orders. Remarkably, an electric field as small as ~0.001 V/Å can simultaneously reverse the polarization and induce an antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition. The associated barrier is exceptionally low (~49 meV/f.u.), yielding a sizable magnetoelectric coefficient of ~0.04 G⋅cm/V. These results highlight a viable strategy for realizing electric-field-driven magnetism in intrinsic two-dimensional multiferroics under experimentally feasible conditions.

---

## Introduction

Electric-field control of magnetism offers a promising route to reduce energy consumption in spintronic and memory devices, paving the way for low-power, non-volatile information technologies that could transform future computing paradigms1–3. To date, two primary mechanisms have been extensively investigated: (i) electric-field-induced magnetization switching4–6, and (ii) electric-field-driven magnetic phase transitions7–10. The former enables binary logic operations through spin-orbit torque-driven reversal of magnetization, whereas the latter involves switching between distinct magnetic phases—such as ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM)—offering dynamic tunability between writable and interference-robust memory states. Realizing such functionality requires material systems where electric polarization and magnetic order are strongly coupled and reversibly tunable under experimentally accessible conditions.

Multiferroics, which simultaneously host two or more ferroic orders—such as magnetism, ferroelectricity, or ferroelasticity—within a single phase11, offer a natural platform for realizing intrinsic magnetoelectric (ME) coupling. However, electric-field-induced magnetic phase transitions in existing multiferroics remain rare, primarily due to the generally weak coupling between electric and magnetic order parameters. As a result, polarization reversal alone is often insufficient to drive a magnetic transition12–22. An alternative strategy leverages van der Waals heterostructures composed of 2D magnets and ferroelectrics, where electric control of magnetism arises from interfacial ME effects6,23–27. However, such heterostructures often suffer from weak interfacial coupling and require precise lattice matching and stacking control, posing significant challenges for scalable fabrication and long-term device stability28. Thus, identifying single-phase 2D multiferroics with strong intrinsic ME coupling has become a central pursuit in the field29–31. Despite increasing interest, such materials remain scarce. Moreover, the substantial switching barriers (>several hundred meV/f.u.) observed in most reported materials demand high electric fields (>0.1 V/Å), creating a major bottleneck for their application in energy-efficient electronics.

In this study, we report four stable 2D bimetallic thio(seleno) phosphate (BMTP) multiferroics, XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au), each exhibiting two inequivalent C2-symmetric phases with opposite in-plane spontaneous polarizations, which helps mitigate depolarization fields. Notably, CuMnP2Se6 features two such C2 phases with distinct magnetic ground states—FM and AFM. An ultralow electric field of ~0.001 V/Å can drive a structural transition between these phases, thereby reversing the polarization and switching the magnetic order simultaneously. The transition is characterized by a remarkably low switching barrier (~49 meV/f.u.) and a sizable ME coupling coefficient (~0.04 G⋅cm/V). These findings demonstrate strong ME coupling and ultralow switching barriers in 2D BMTPs, highlighting their potential as a promising platform for electric-field control of magnetic phase transitions under experimentally accessible conditions.

---

## Results

In-plane polarization in CuMnP2Se6
The BMTPs with the general formula XYP2(S/Se)6 (X, Y = transition metals), crystallize in van der Waals layered structures and represent a versatile family of emerging piezoelectric, ferroelectric, and multiferroic materials32–35. Their compositional flexibility—achieved by varying X and Y elements such as Cu, Ag, In, Cr, and V—enables systematic tuning of electronic, ferroelectric, and magnetic properties36–39. Dimensional reduction to monolayers via mechanical exfoliation offers an effective pathway to tailor ferroic behaviors40–43, with improved control over polarization and magnetic states.

A prototypical 2D BMTP structure, exemplified by CuCrP2S6, consists of metal cations intercalated within a hexagonal framework composed of ethane-like [P2S6]4− units with C3 symmetry. The Cu1+ and Cr3+ cations alternately occupy interstitial sites, forming a secondary honeycomb sublattice. Each Cr3+ ion is centered within an octahedron of six S2− ligands, accounting for the magnetic behavior, while the out-of-plane displacement of Cu1+ ion gives rise to spontaneous polarization44. The out-of-plane (OOP) polarization switching proceeds through a nonpolar (NP) intermediate phase which possesses D3 symmetry. Notably, a broad range of 2D BMTPs can be derived by substituting different transition-metal species into this structural motif36–39,45.

To further explore the structural landscape of 2D BMTP family, we performed ab initio structure searches for CuMnP2Se6 using the CALYPSO method46–51. We selected Mn as the Y-site transition metal because Mn3+ possesses a high-spin d4 electron configuration. In an MnSe6 octahedral environment, the Mn3+ ion adopts a t2g3 eg1 configuration, which is well known to produce a strong Jahn-Teller instability (Supplementary Fig. 1). The singly occupied eg orbital (dz2 or dx2−y2) directly overlaps with the ligand p orbitals, leading to pronounced structural distortion of MnSe6 octahedra, involving tetragonal compression or tetragonal elongation (Supplementary Table 1). This situation stands in sharp contrast to other 2D BMTPs such as CuCrP2Se6 (Cr3+, t2g3), CuVP2Se6 (V3+, t2g2) and CuFeP2Se6 (Fe3+, t2g3 eg2), where the transition-metal ions are Jahn-Teller inactive. Consequently, the strong Jahn-Teller activity of Mn3+ may facilitate the emergence of new structural prototypes that are inaccessible to other transition metals.

As expected, two low-energy polar prototypes with C2 symmetry were identified, referred to as the D-type and C-type phases, characterized by the formation of Cu-Mn dimer-like units and -Cu-Mn-Cu-Mn-chain-like configurations, respectively. In contrast to conventional BMTP structures, where the X cation typically displaces vertically from the center of its octahedron, the X ion in both newly identified phases remains centered, accompanied by slight in-plane displacements. These displacements give rise to spontaneous in-plane polarization. Specifically, the D-type and C-type structures exhibit opposite in-plane polarization directions along [110] and [110], respectively. This behavior stands in sharp contrast to most previously reported 2D BMTP multiferroics, which typically display OOP polarization36,44.

The distinct polarization behavior in these systems arises from two key factors: Jahn-Teller activity and symmetry-forbidden s-d coupling44. The Jahn-Teller active Mn3+ ion (t2g3 eg1) lifts the eg orbital degeneracy, leading to tetragonal compression in the D-type phase and tetragonal elongation in the C-type phase (Supplementary Table 1). These distortions generate an in-plane anisotropic local potential, which drives lateral Cu displacement. In contrast, in BMTP compounds such as CuCrP2S6, where the Jahn-Teller effect is weak, the nearly symmetric crystal field fails to create such a gradient potential, thereby suppressing in-plane polarization.

Meanwhile, the local approximate Oh symmetry around the Cu+ ion in CuMnP2Se6 forbids s-d coupling because the s and d orbitals belong to different irreducible representations (Supplementary Table 2). This symmetry-forbidden s-d hybridization contrasts with the symmetry-allowed s-d coupling in CuInP2S6, which drives the OOP polarization44. This forbidden s-d coupling in CuMnP2Se6 is further supported by the projected density of states (PDOS) and band-decomposed charge density (Supplementary Fig. 2). Therefore, the combination of strong Jahn-Teller distortion and symmetry-forbidden s-d coupling collectively determines the emergence and stabilization of in-plane polarization in CuMnP2Se6. A more detailed discussion is provided in the Supplementary Information.

High-throughput screening and identification of in-plane ferroelectric phases and magnetic ground states
Having identified four structural prototypes, we employed high-throughput first-principles calculations to systematically investigate the possibility of D-type and C-type structures within this material family. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, we considered compounds with the formula XYP2(S/Se)6 (X=Cu, Ag, Au; Y=Mn, Tc), generated via targeted elemental substitution. The X-site elements (Cu, Ag, Au) were chosen as monovalent cation owing to their good displacive nature and can easily displace from the octahedral center, thus generating ferroelectric polarization. The Y-site transition metals were selected to ensure a high-spin t2g3 eg1 configuration (e.g., Mn3+ and Tc3+), which naturally leads to Jahn-Teller activity and strong coupling among orbital, lattice, and spin degrees of freedom.

A total of 48 candidate structures were initially generated based on the four structural prototypes. After full structural relaxation, 5 OOP-polarized phases were found to be unstable and spontaneously transformed into NP phases. The potential energy profile of Cu-ion displacement further confirms the energetic preference for the NP phase (Supplementary Fig. 3). Consequently, the final dataset comprises 43 stable configurations: 7 OOP, 12 NP, 12 D-type, and 12 C-type phases (Fig. 2a). Among these, all XYP2(S/Se)6 compounds in the D-type and C-type phases, except AgMnP2Se6, possess lower energies than their NP and OOP counterparts (Supplementary Table 3). Because the total energies of AgMnP2Se6 in different prototypes are nearly degenerate, indicating a structurally marginal system, it was excluded from subsequent phonon calculations.

Phonon spectrum calculations reveal that CuMnP2(S/Se)6 and AuMnP2(S/Se)6 are dynamically stable in both D-type and C-type configurations, whereas AgMnP2S6 is stable only in the C-type configuration (Supplementary Figs. 4, 5). We then determined the magnetic ground states of the dynamically stable compounds, excluding AgMnP2S6 since only its C-type phase is stable and no meaningful comparison between two polar phases can be made. For the remaining systems, we considered one FM and two possible AFM configurations (Supplementary Fig. 6). Interestingly, unlike other compounds where both polar phases prefer AFM ordering, CuMnP2Se6 displays two polar phases with different magnetic ground states—one FM and one AFM (Fig. 2b). This unique behavior allows an electric-field-induced polarization reversal to simultaneously trigger a magnetic phase transition between FM and AFM states. Consequently, we focus our subsequent discussion on CuMnP2Se6.

Distinct structural motifs, electronic properties and magnetic ground states in D-type and C-type CuMnP2Se6
Figure 3a and b show schematic structural diagrams of the D-type and C-type phases of CuMnP2Se6 in a 2×2×1 supercell, with the P and Se atoms omitted for clarity. In the D-type phase, Cu and Mn atoms form dimer-like units with a nearest-neighbor distance of 3.43 Å, and the distance between neighboring dimers is 3.82 Å. In the C-type phase, Cu and Mn atoms form chain-like units with a nearest-neighbor distance of 3.64 Å along the chain, and the distance between neighboring chains is 3.75 Å. The C-type phase is slightly lower in energy than the D-type phase by ~4 meV/f.u.

The cohesive energy of CuMnP2Se6 is calculated using the equation Ecoh = (Etot − ECu − EMn − 2EP − 6ESe)/10, where Etot is the total energy of 2D CuMnP2Se6, and ECu, EMn, EP, and ESe are the total energies of isolated Cu, Mn, P, and Se atoms, respectively. The cohesive energies for both D-type and C-type phases are similar, ~ -3.92 eV/atom, suggesting that both structures are thermodynamically stable and potentially synthesizable. Furthermore, Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations at 100 K confirm the thermal stability and in-plane long-range polarized order of CuMnP2Se6 (Supplementary Fig. 7).

The spin-polarized band structures show that both the D-type and C-type phases are semiconductors with indirect band gaps of 0.18 eV and 0.16 eV, respectively (Fig. 3c, d). Spin-orbit coupling has a negligible effect on the electronic structure and is therefore excluded from subsequent calculations (Supplementary Fig. 8). Spin density calculations show that the spin moments are mainly localized on Mn ions (Supplementary Fig. 9). The PDOS confirms that the spin polarization near the Fermi level mainly comes from Mn 3d orbitals. The formal spin moments for Mn and Cu are 4 μB and 0 μB, respectively, consistent with their expected valence states of Mn3+ and Cu1+. The overlap between the Mn 3d and Cu 3d orbitals is observed below the Fermi level in PDOS (Supplementary Fig. 10). In fact, the overlap originates from the strong hybridization of Mn 3d-Se 4p and Cu 3d-Se 4p states, making the Cu and Mn d states appear to overlap.

In the D-type phase, the valence band maximum is primarily derived from Mn dx2−y2 orbitals, while the conduction band minimum mainly originates from Mn dz2 orbitals (Fig. 3e). In contrast, the C-type phase shows the opposite orbital contributions to the valence and conduction bands (Fig. 3f). The calculated onsite energies of Mn d orbitals (Supplementary Table 4) confirm that the dx2−y2 orbital lies lower in energy than the dz2 orbital in the D-type phase, whereas the reverse holds for the C-type phase. This distinct orbital ordering enhances Mn dx2−y2 -Se pxy hybridization in the D-type phase and Mn dz2 -Se pz hybridization in the C-type phase (Fig. 3g, h; Supplementary Fig. 11). Structurally, the D-type phase exhibits tetragonal compression, which energetically favors the formation of Mn-Cu dimer-like units, whereas the C-type phase shows tetragonal elongation, stabilizing a chain-like -Mn-Cu-Mn-Cu- arrangement (Supplementary Table 1; Fig. 3a, b). This structural response reflects the system’s tendency to minimize total energy under different orbital hybridization conditions. In turn, these distinct structural configurations tend to modulate the Mn-Mn exchange pathways, which may lead to different magnetic ground states in the two phases.

The spin Hamiltonian is defined as H = − ∑i,j J1 Si Sj − ∑i,k J2 Si Sk, where J1 and J2 are the nearest-neighbor and next-nearest neighbor magnetic exchange parameters between Mn ions, respectively22,52–54. The summation i, j, and k run over all the Mn sites. S is the formal magnetic moment of Mn ion. The positive and negative J values represent the FM and AFM coupling, respectively. By energy mapping analysis on the considered magnetic configurations (Supplementary Fig. 6), the calculated J1 and J2 for the D-type are 4.70 meV and 1.30 meV, respectively, indicating the FM ground state. In contrast, the calculated J1 and J2 for the C-type are 4.67 meV and -4.72 meV, respectively, indicating the AFM ground state. Monte Carlo simulations show that the magnetic critical temperature for FM D-type and AFM C-type phases are ~31 K and ~18 K, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 12).

We further investigated the impact of the Hubbard U parameter on magnetic ordering and orbital-level splitting for both D-type and C-type phases, finding that the overall qualitative trends and key conclusions are robust over a broad range of U values (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6).

Electric-field-induced magnetic switching in CuMnP2Se6
Berry phase calculations yield an in-plane polarization of 0.9 × 10−10 C/m along the [110] direction for the D-type phase and 0.7 × 10−10 C/m along the [110] direction for the C-type phase (Supplementary Figs. 13, 14). Born effective charge analysis55,56 gives corresponding values of 0.4 × 10−10 C/m for the D-type phase and 0.2 × 10−10 C/m for the C-type phase, in good agreement with those obtained from the Berry-phase method. These values are larger than those reported for other DTMPs12,36,57,58, such as AgBiP2Se6 (1.2 × 10−12 C/m), CuCrP2S6 (0.79 × 10−12 C/m), AuZrP2S6 (9.74 × 10−12 C/m), and comparable to other 2D multiferroics13,16,59–61, such as (CrBr3)Li (0.92 × 10−10 C/m), and γ-AlOOH (0.85 × 10−10 C/m).

The polarization in both the D-type and C-type phases can only be switched by 120° through an in-plane rotation of 120° or 240° (Fig. 4a, b; Supplementary Fig. 15a, b). This process can also be understood as a lateral displacement of Cu ions. The corresponding energy barriers for ferroelectric switching are ~36 meV/f.u. for the D-type phase and ~32 meV/f.u. for the C-type phase. In contrast, a 180° polarization reversal within the same phase (either D-type or C-type) is prohibited, as the positions of Cu and Mn ions cannot be interchanged directly.

However, 180° polarization reversal remains feasible through an electric-field-induced phase transition between the D-type and C-type structures, accompanied by the migration or removal of Cu atoms (Fig. 4c; Supplementary Fig. 15c). Specifically, reversing the applied electric field—e.g., from [110] to [110]—can trigger a transition between the two phases, owing to their opposite polarization orientations. This electric-field-driven structural transformation simultaneously induces a magnetic phase transition, owing to the distinct magnetic ground states of the D-type and C-type structures. Figure 4c illustrates the energy barrier associated with this phase transition, which proceeds via an intermediate structure that closely resembles the D configuration and can be regarded as the NP phase (Supplementary Fig. 16). The calculated barriers for both D-to-C and C-to-D transitions are nearly identical, ~49 meV/f.u. This value is nearly an order of magnitude lower than those reported for other 2D multiferroics exhibiting electric-field-induced magnetic transitions29–31. Notably, the D-to-C transition can also be triggered by applying tensile strain (Supplementary Fig. 17).

The ME coupling coefficient can be estimated as α ≈ μ0 |ΔM|/Ec, where μ0 is the vacuum permeability, ΔM is the magnetization change per unit cell associated with polarization switching, and Ec is the coercive electric field62. As is well known, a direct evaluation of Ec from first-principles is very challenging, since in real ferroelectric materials, polarization reversal is typically dominated by domain-wall motion and defect-mediated processes rather than homogeneous switching, and Ec is also strongly temperature dependent63. Therefore, we adopted a more reasonable reference value based on experimentally accessible ferroelectric systems to estimate Ec. The values of energy barrier (4.9 meV/atom) and polarization (13 μC/cm2 for the D-type phase and 9 μC/cm2 for the C-type phase, assuming an effective thickness of 7 Å) in CuMnP2Se6 are comparable to those reported for ferroelectric Hf(Zr)1+xO2 thin films (7.3 meV/atom; 22.5 μC/cm2)64. Thus, we adopt the experimentally reported coercive field of Hf(Zr)1+xO2, 65 kV/cm, to estimate the ME coupling coefficient of CuMnP2Se6. This yields α ≈ 0.04 G⋅cm/V, which exceeds those of bulk multiferroic Fe/BaTiO3 (~0.01 G⋅cm/V)62, and 2D WReCl36 (~0.02 G⋅cm/V)29, indicating the strong ME coupling.

To evaluate the feasibility of in-plane electric-field-driven structural transitions between the D-type and C-type phases, we investigate the field-dependent total energies of both configurations (Fig. 4d). The two phases exhibit opposite responses: an electric field along the [110] direction stabilizes the C-type phase, while a field along [110] favors the D-type phase. Strikingly, an ultralow field of ~0.001 V/Å along [110] is sufficient to render the D-type phase more stable than its C-type counterpart, enabling an electric-field-induced C-to-D transition. The critical field lies well within experimentally accessible limits8,65, highlighting the potential of CuMnP2Se6 for practical multifunctional device applications.

In summary, we identify four stable 2D multiferroics of the form XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au), each exhibiting two inequivalent C2-symmetric polar phases with opposite in-plane polarization directions, based on crystal structure prediction and high-throughput first-principles calculations. Jahn-Teller activity and symmetry-forbidden s-d coupling are identified as the two primary driving forces for the emergence of in-plane polarization in these systems. Notably, in CuMnP2Se6, the two polar phases differ not only in their polarization orientation but also in their magnetic ground states (FM and AFM), enabling electric-field-driven switching of both ferroic orders. The ultralow energy barrier (~49 meV/f.u.) and critical switching field (~0.001 V Å−1) render these coupled transitions experimentally accessible. These findings demonstrate a viable route for electric control of magnetism in single-phase 2D multiferroics and provide new insights into ferroic coupling in the BMTP family, with promising implications for low-power, non-volatile device applications. This work also opens a promising avenue for exploring ultralow-field electric control of magnetism enabled by Jahn-Teller-assisted phase-transition mechanisms.

---

## Methods

First-principles calculations were performed based on density functional theory66 via the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)67,68 using the generalized gradient approximation with the projected augmented wave method69 with a 450 eV plane-wave energy cutoff. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof function was adopted for the exchange-correlation functional70. A Γ-centered k-point grid of 11 × 11 × 1 was applied for sampling the Brillouin zone. The energy and force threshold for structural optimization are 10−7 eV and 0.001 eV/Å, respectively. An effective Hubbard U of 4 eV for Mn 3d, Cu 3d and Tc 4d orbitals71,72 was applied following the Dudarev formulation73. Phonon spectra were calculated using the finite displacement method implemented in the PHONOPY code74. The temperature-dependent effective potential method was used to determine the influence of thermal effects on phonon spectra75. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations were performed utilizing the Nosé-Hoover chain thermostat for 5 ps with a time step of 1 fs with 3 × 3 × 1 supercell. Climbing image nudged elastic band calculations76 were performed to determine the energy barriers for ferroelectric switching. The polarization was estimated using the Berry phase approach77. An in-plane electric field was applied by imposing a finite homogeneous field using the perturbation expression after discretization approach78,79. The maximally localized Wannier functions are constructed by using the WANNIER90 code80.

The particle-swarm optimization method within the evolutionary algorithm, as implemented in the CALYPSO code46–51, was employed to search for the lowest-energy structures of the CuMnP2Se6 monolayer. Unit cells containing one and two formula units were considered. In the initial generation, random structures with specific symmetries were constructed by generating atomic coordinates through crystallographic symmetry operations. Local optimizations were carried out using the VASP code67,68 with the conjugate-gradient method and terminated when the Gibbs free-energy change was smaller than 1 × 10−4 eV per cell. After each generation, 40% of the low-energy structures were selected to construct the next generation through particle swarm optimization, while the remaining 60% were randomly generated. A structure fingerprinting technique based on the bond-characterization matrix was employed to avoid duplication and enhance population diversity, which is crucial for efficient global searching. In total, the search typically sampled 1200 structures (40 generations × 30 structures).

### Reviewer 1

The authors J. Chen et al., in their manuscript “ Phase-Transition-Induced Ferroelectric and Magnetic Switching in Two-Dimensional CuMnP2Se6 under Ultra-Low Electric Fields”, have investigated four compounds XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au) belonging to the family of bimetallic thio(seleno)phosphates using density functional theory based calculations. Their main observations are the presence of in-plane electric polarization in these four compounds as opposed to the out-of-plane polarization reported earlier for other members of the family. The authors also report that a tiny electric field can be used to switch the polarization direction in CuMnP2Se6 along with the magnetic order.
I observe some serious issues with the conclusions drawn here by the authors which I outline below.
1. The non-polar intermediate state D3, between the D-type and C-type phases, is metallic (see Fig. S11). Therefore, an electric field cannot be used to switch the direction of polarization. Another related question is when the non-polar D3 phase is metallic, how was the polarization quantum calculated? It is not possible to calculate it by following the standard procedure.
2. The AIMD snapshots at 300K after 10 ps for both D and C-type (Fig. S4) show a significant change in the bond lengths which is the primary requirement for the structure to be called D-type or C-type (Fig. 3 (a) & (b)). Thus, at 300K, D and C-type phases of the structure don’t survive and there should be no net in-plane polarization given the loss of order in the bond lengths of the structures.
3. Why a weak Jahn-Teller effect will give rise to out-of-plane polarization whereas a strong Jahn-Teller effect will give rise to in-plane polarization is not clear at all. The orbital resolved DOS presented in Fig. S7 shows Mn dz2 and dx2-y2 orbitals both present below the Fermi level. A strong Jahn-Teller effect would have split these two orbitals widely.
4. How does distinct orbital ordering in C and D-type phases lead to the respective structural distortions? How do they give rise to different magnetic ground states for C and D-type phases? No explanation is provided. Moreover, the DOS in Fig. 3 (e) shows substantial contribution of both dz2 and dx2-y2 orbitals in the valence band whereas the band character plot shows dominant dx2-y2 contribution.
5. The claim that there is no bonding like interaction between Cu and Mn is not very convincing. There seems to be a very strong overlap between Cu and Mn d states in the valence band (as seen in PDOS of Fig. 3(c), 3(d) and S7) which directly indicates a strong hybridization between Cu and Mn. The ELF plot also shows some bonding like behaviour particularly in the C-type structure. Also, the crystal field around Cu changes in a similar manner as that around Mn typical for a Cu-Mn bonding interaction (see Fig. 1(c), 1(d)). The non-polar phase PDOS (Fig. S11(b)) also shows a very strong Cu-Mn hybridization.
6. If Cu-d orbitals do not hybridize with Mn-d orbitals as claimed, why doesn’t it exhibit s-d interaction and hence, an out-of-plane displacement as is the case with the materials without an eg electron (e.g., CuCrP2S6).
7. How are the temperatures for phonon calculations in Fig. S2 decided? What about the dynamic stability at higher temperatures? The last phonon spectrum for AuMnP2S6 seems to have imaginary frequencies.
8. There are a couple of typos. ( ‘insensitive’ instead of ‘sensitive’ and ‘eg’ instead of ‘t2g’ in the Supplementary mat.).
Finally, I would like to mention that no new concept has been presented in this manuscript. The concept as well as the analysis is exactly similar to the work by Meiling Xu et al. , Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 067602 (2020) (ref. [29] of the manuscript). Only the compound studied is different.
In view of the above serious issues, I can not recommend the manuscript for publication in the highly reputed journal Nature Communications.

The research focus on the electric field control of magnetic phase transitions, specially in cases where the necessary electric fields are small for practical reasons. Those are already the methods necessary within first principles to access the viability of the materials experimentally. ## Paper

## Abstract

Low-field electric control of magnetic phase transitions is critical for the development of energy-efficient spintronic and non-volatile memory technologies. Yet, the weak magnetoelectric coupling in most known two-dimensional multiferroics hinders their practical implementation. Here, using crystal structure prediction and high-throughput first-principles calculations, we identify four previously unexplored bimetallic thio(seleno) phosphate multiferroics, XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X=Cu, Au), all exhibiting robust in-plane spontaneous polarization—contrasting with the predominantly out-of-plane behavior in this material family—which effectively mitigates depolarization effects. In particular, CuMnP2Se6 hosts two stable C2-symmetric ferroelectric phases with opposite in-plane polarizations and distinct magnetic orders. Remarkably, an electric field as small as ~0.001 V/Å can simultaneously reverse the polarization and induce an antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition. The associated barrier is exceptionally low (~49 meV/f.u.), yielding a sizable magnetoelectric coefficient of ~0.04 G⋅cm/V. These results highlight a viable strategy for realizing electric-field-driven magnetism in intrinsic two-dimensional multiferroics under experimentally feasible conditions.

## Introduction

Electric-field control of magnetism offers a promising route to reduce energy consumption in spintronic and memory devices, paving the way for low-power, non-volatile information technologies that could transform future computing paradigms1–3. To date, two primary mechanisms have been extensively investigated: (i) electric-field-induced magnetization switching4–6, and (ii) electric-field-driven magnetic phase transitions7–10. The former enables binary logic operations through spin-orbit torque-driven reversal of magnetization, whereas the latter involves switching between distinct magnetic phases—such as ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM)—offering dynamic tunability between writable and interference-robust memory states. Realizing such functionality requires material systems where electric polarization and magnetic order are strongly coupled and reversibly tunable under experimentally accessible conditions.

Multiferroics, which simultaneously host two or more ferroic orders—such as magnetism, ferroelectricity, or ferroelasticity—within a single phase11, offer a natural platform for realizing intrinsic magnetoelectric (ME) coupling. However, electric-field-induced magnetic phase transitions in existing multiferroics remain rare, primarily due to the generally weak coupling between electric and magnetic order parameters. As a result, polarization reversal alone is often insufficient to drive a magnetic transition12–22. An alternative strategy leverages van der Waals heterostructures composed of 2D magnets and ferroelectrics, where electric control of magnetism arises from interfacial ME effects6,23–27. However, such heterostructures often suffer from weak interfacial coupling and require precise lattice matching and stacking control, posing significant challenges for scalable fabrication and long-term device stability28. Thus, identifying single-phase 2D multiferroics with strong intrinsic ME coupling has become a central pursuit in the field29–31. Despite increasing interest, such materials remain scarce. Moreover, the substantial switching barriers (>several hundred meV/f.u.) observed in most reported materials demand high electric fields (>0.1 V/Å), creating a major bottleneck for their application in energy-efficient electronics.

In this study, we report four stable 2D bimetallic thio(seleno) phosphate (BMTP) multiferroics, XMnP2(S/Se)6 (X = Cu, Au), each exhibiting two inequivalent C2-symmetric phases with opposite in-plane spontaneous polarizations, which helps mitigate depolarization fields. Notably, CuMnP2Se6 features two such C2 phases with distinct magnetic ground states—FM and AFM. An ultralow electric field of ~0.001 V/Å can drive a structural transition between these phases, thereby reversing the polarization and switching the magnetic order simultaneously. The transition is characterized by a remarkably low switching barrier (~49 meV/f.u.) and a sizable ME coupling coefficient (~0.04 G⋅cm/V). These findings demonstrate strong ME coupling and ultralow switching barriers in 2D BMTPs, highlighting their potential as a promising platform for electric-field control of magnetic phase transitions under experimentally accessible conditions.
